messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 71
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Oceania
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Painter
  trauma_type: Terrorism
  pcl5: 48

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Reassurance Seeking: I keep asking others to reassure me that I am okay, Emotion Control: I try hard to control my emotions, Avoid Going Out: Going out
  Memory: Bodily Reenactment: When memories come to mind of what happened, I feel my body is in the same position as when the frightening event occurred., Vivid Memory: My memories of the frightening event are very clear and detailed., Uncontrolled Access: The memory forces its way into my mind when I do not want it to
  Negative Appraisals: Can't Rely on Self: I can't rely on myself, Can't Rely on Others: I can't rely on other people, World is Dangerous: The world is a dangerous place

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Mika is a 71-year-old man of Oceanian background who has spent most of his adult life working as a painter, taking jobs in apartment buildings, storefronts, and church halls across his part of the city. He lives alone and had been used to a routine built around early mornings, steady handwork, and long hours moving through public spaces without much thought. The change in him began after a terrorist attack that occurred during an ordinary workday, when he was painting inside a commercial building near a crowded pedestrian area. He had gone out to get coffee and was passing near the entrance when the blast happened. What stayed with him was not an abstract idea of danger but the exact physical fact of it: the violent force, the abrupt drop of his body, the way he ended up twisted on the ground and unable for several seconds to understand whether he was alive. He remembers the smell in the air, the sound of people screaming, and the sight of debris scattered across the pavement with a clarity that still unsettles him. In his mind there is nothing blurred or softened by time; the memory arrives sharp, complete, and unwanted.

In the weeks afterward, Mika found that the attack did not remain in the past in the way he expected it would. At odd moments, without invitation, the scene forced itself into his mind. He could be rinsing brushes, waiting in line for supplies, or sitting quietly at home, and suddenly he was back there. What frightened him especially was how much his body seemed to join the memory. When it came, he felt himself pulled into the same position he had been in after the explosion, as if his torso were bracing against the pavement again and his muscles had remembered the exact angle of impact. He would stiffen or hunch without meaning to, caught for a moment in the posture of that day. Because the memory was so vivid and detailed, he did not experience it as a faded recollection but as something close and immediate, and he came to feel that the world outside his apartment could turn lethal without warning.

Over time, Mika had come to believe that neither he nor anyone else could be relied upon. He was disturbed by how completely he had lost control of his body and mind during the attack, and afterward he took that as evidence that he could not trust himself to cope if something happened again. At the same time, the fact that an ordinary public place had become the site of terrorism left him certain that other people could not keep him safe either. He spoke as if danger were woven into everyday life now, not confined to particular places or circumstances. Sidewalks, transit stops, busy storefronts, and office lobbies all felt exposed.

His attempts to manage this have narrowed his life. He tries hard to control his emotions, especially around other people, keeping his face composed and cutting off any sign that he is frightened or overwhelmed. When he feels himself react, he clamps down and goes quiet. He also keeps asking others to reassure him that he is okay. If a neighbor notices he looks shaken, or if a former coworker calls, Mika finds himself asking in slightly different ways whether he seems all right, whether what he is feeling is normal, whether he is “still okay.” The reassurance settles him only briefly. More and more, he has limited going out unless he feels he has to. For a man whose work once depended on moving from one job site to another, this has had practical consequences. He has turned down painting work in larger buildings and busy public-facing spaces because leaving home feels like stepping back into vulnerability. Small jobs have become difficult to accept if they require travel through crowded areas, and his income and contact with others have both shrunk.

By the time he sought help, Mika had been living in a tightened, watchful way for months. He spent much of his time at home with his tools neatly arranged, as if preserving a work life he no longer moved through freely. What finally brought him in was not a single new symptom but the recognition that his world had become very small and that he was organizing his days around staying inside, holding himself together, and asking others to tell him he was safe. He is afraid that the danger he senses everywhere is simply the truth of the world now, and that if he lets his guard down he will be caught helpless again. At the same time, he says he wants to be able to take a painting job, walk out the door, and trust his own mind enough to live like a person rather than like someone waiting for the next attack.
